name: Voice surgery (cricothyroid approximation)

lead: Cricothyroid approximation (CTA) is a voice surgery that raises your speaking pitch. The payoff people want is a higher voice, and the pitch change is measurable after surgery. It has mainly been used for voice feminisation in transgender women.

The surgeon moves the cricoid and thyroid cartilages closer together, which lengthens and tenses the vocal folds. A 2017 systematic review of pitch-raising surgery found mixed results, and a 2025 meta-analysis reported that surgery generally produced larger and more lasting pitch gains than voice therapy. Fewer clinicians perform CTA now than Wendler glottoplasty.

paras: CTA is performed by a surgeon as a one-off operation, not a routine you repeat. It is sometimes considered by people for whom voice therapy has not given enough change. Newer techniques have largely replaced it, so availability is limited.

It is irreversible surgery. Reported risks include a voice locked into falsetto, loss of loudness or quality, swallowing or breathing problems, infection and scarring, and outcomes may decline over time.

social.title: Demand grows for gender-affirming voice surgery, but access remains limited

angle.text: Cricothyroid approximation pulls the laryngeal cartilages together to tension the vocal folds, giving a higher speaking pitch that can be measured after surgery. It has mainly been used for voice feminisation, and newer techniques have largely replaced it.

lead: Cricothyroid approximation (CTA) is a voice surgery that raises vocal pitch by drawing the cricoid and thyroid cartilages of the larynx closer together, which stretches and tightens the vocal folds. People seek it so that their speaking voice sits higher and reads as more feminine, since voice is one of the first things listeners register about a person, alongside the face.[1][2]

CTA belongs to a family of pitch-raising operations (phonosurgery). Others work by shortening the vocal folds or reducing their mass, for example Wendler glottoplasty and laser reduction glottoplasty.[3] Voice therapy is generally the first step, and clinicians describe surgery as an option for people who do not reach a satisfying voice through non-surgical means.[2]

Published reviews compare the techniques. A 2022 review notes that the fundamental frequency is raised maximally and stays stable after glottoplasty compared with CTA, which is one reason glottoplasty is more commonly performed today.[1] A 2017 meta-analysis of 13 studies compared tension, shortening and mass-reduction approaches on pre- and post-operative pitch.[3]

paras: Pitch depends on vocal fold length, thickness and tension. Reviews describe higher pitch as the result of folds that are shorter, thinner and tighter, and CTA targets the tension part of that equation.[1] Surgeons approximate the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, which increases tension on the folds.[1][3]

Voice feminisation surgery as a group includes CTA, Wendler glottoplasty, laser reduction glottoplasty, feminisation laryngoplasty, laser tuning and resonance surgery. Voice surgery is one of several non-genital procedures, alongside facial feminisation surgery, listed in overviews of gender-affirming care.[4][5]

A 2006 review of transgender voice management reported that speech and language therapy can produce an acceptable fundamental frequency and shape other communication behaviours, and that laryngeal surgery such as CTA has a role for people who do not achieve an acceptable voice by non-surgical means.[2] The same review noted that little information existed at that time on patient satisfaction and quality of life.[2]

Wikipedia reports that CTA can leave some patients with a falsetto-like voice, that results may decline over time, and that fewer clinicians perform it now than Wendler glottoplasty. A 2025 meta-analysis summarised there found that surgery tended to produce larger and longer-lasting pitch gains than voice therapy alone.

A 2017 systematic review in the Journal of Voice assessed the effectiveness of pitch-raising surgery in male-to-female transsexual patients.[6] A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery searched six databases, found 29 studies, and included 13 with pre- and post-operative acoustic analysis, grouping techniques by mechanism (tension, shortening, mass reduction).[3]

A 2022 review of gender-affirming laryngeal and voice surgery concluded that fundamental frequency is raised maximally and remains stable after glottoplasty compared with CTA.[1] A 2017 update on surgical treatment for transgender patients lists voice surgery among the male-to-female procedures.[5] A 2021 Laryngoscope paper examined insurance coverage for gender-affirming voice surgery and therapy.[7]

Reported risks across voice feminisation surgery include reduced voice quality and loudness, swallowing or breathing problems, sore throat, infection and scarring. Vocal fold scarring is recognised in the voice-surgery literature as a major cause of voice disorders after laryngeal surgery or trauma.[8]

A Canadian news item shared on Lemmy reported that demand for gender-affirming voice surgery is growing while access remains limited, with only a small number of otolaryngologists performing it; one surgeon described belonging to a group of about 70 surgeons worldwide doing these procedures.[9]
